changelog.change: Initial canonical codebook. All definitions transcribed verbatim from Zhang et al. (2025). Inherited meso-level definitions (Zagal et al. [87], Sousa & Oliveira [74], King et al. [39], Hadan et al. [23], Dahlan & Susanty [12].
Improve code book structure and ordering.
Add preliminary global rules and cross-verify definitions.
Final version prior to pilot labeling. Fix inconsistencies.
Add Boundary Rules, Worked Examples and counters after coding 25 reviews

global_rules.statement: One review is one unit. Assign each applicable meso label at most once per review, regardless of how many times the pattern appears in the text.
Assign a label only when the review describes a game mechanic or design behaviour. Never assign from rating, tone, or general dissatisfaction alone.
Record the exact quoted span that triggered each label. A label with no recorded span is invalid and must be removed.
Assign the label the recorded span satisfies. Never assign because the game is known to contain the pattern, or because the pattern usually co-occurs with one already assigned.

Every entry in a label's indicators list is an instance of that pattern, whether tagged [low-level], [dp-combo], or [indicators]. A span that names an instance assigns its meso label; a meso label assigns its high-level class. Alternate definitions (Alt. def.) are restatements of the meso definition, not instances.

global_rules.statement: Assign labels irrespective of the reviewer's approval or disapproval. A five-star review praising daily login rewards receives Daily Rewards.
global_rules.worked_example_text:
This game is a ridiculous amount of fun and I haven't had it crash yet. There's a lot of strategy involved if you want to rank up but you can just tool around and still have a good time. Be aware; there's a fair amount of waiting if you don't want to pay to speed things up. Edit (almost a decade later): just got back into playing and it's even more fun with the builder base addition. It cuts the wait time down on gameplay and involves real tactical thought.

Labels: Playing by Appointment, Pay to Progress

global_rules.statement: Code the mechanic described, not the reviewer's evaluation of it. "Generous battle pass" and "predatory battle pass" both describe a battle pass.
When two labels both fit and no boundary rule separates them, assign both.
If a game mechanic is not clear from the review's context, an external search can be used. Justify the search and tag the search query along with the review.
global_rules.worked_example_text:
Tired of game play changing for the worse. There used to be a variety of mini games. Now it's candy crush with a side of farming/town building. They made the boosters in the mini game worse and seems like most people did not get compensated as they said. I swear the golden ticket was cheaper or lasted a longer amount of time. global_rules.statement: Where the span attributes the described behaviour to a bug, glitch, error, or technical fault, assign NONE, even if the behaviour would otherwise satisfy a label. Dark patterns are design choices; malfunctions are not. Applies only where the bug attribution is attached to the specific behaviour being coded. A general statement that a game is buggy, glitchy, or broken does not suppress labels on other spans in the same review.

R12. Code only mechanics the span describes as present in the game. Requests, suggestions, wishes, and hypotheticals about mechanics the game does not have ("they should add…", "make us watch an ad to get coins", "if only there were…") are not codable, even where the named mechanic matches a label.

high_level_classes.name: Temporal
high_level_classes.canonical_definition: Temporal DPs manipulate the amount of time spent on gameplay, i.e., expected versus actual time, leading players to feel that their time has been unfairly exploited [87].

high_level_classes.name: Monetary
high_level_classes.canonical_definition: Monetary DPs cause players to unexpectedly invest more financial resources, ultimately causing them to regret or lose track of their expenditures [87].
high_level_classes.definition_citation: Zhang et al. 2025, §3.4 (verbatim; after Zagal et al. [87])

high_level_classes.name: Social
high_level_classes.canonical_definition: Social DPs exploit players’ social connections from the real world and in-game to deceive or manipulate them, thereby putting their social standing and relationships at risk [74, 87].

high_level_classes.name: Psychological
high_level_classes.canonical_definition: Psychological DPs and practices manipulate players’ minds, emotions, and cognition, inducing them to make poor decisions through psychological tricks [74].
high_level_classes.definition_citation: Zhang et al. 2025, §3.4 (verbatim; after Sousa & Oliveira [74])

high_level_classes.name: Technical
high_level_classes.canonical_definition: The Technical pattern, deceives users or players by obscuring or misrepresenting the technical aspects of the game application.

labels.canonical_definition: Requires players play at specific times (and or dates) as defined by the game, rather than the players. When mechanics result in player playing according to the schedules the game offers, rather than their personal desires (an obligation).
indicators: (Alt. def.) (Hadan et al. 2024): “Patterns that forces players to adhere to the game’s schedule.”

Evil Battle Pass (Zhang et al.): “Players are required to spend excessive time completing tasks, risking expiration of the battle pass and loss of rewards, even if they have paid for it in advance.” [low-level]

Wait to Play (Hadan et al. 2024): “Patterns that impose arbitrary wait times on players through in-game timers.”
darkpattern.games: “In-game timers that make you arbitrarily wait for something.” [low-level]

Trapping starter kits: This pattern particularly entices new players to log in and play continuously for the first few
days after creating new accounts. These designs often use in-game rewards as incentives, creating
a situation where new players lose the opportunity to obtain these rewards if they fail to log in and
complete tasks within the specified timeframe. [dp-combo]

boundary_rules.rule: Zagal et al.: “Nullified if completing appointments is not required for progress. In other words, when appointment is combined with progress it becomes dark.”

Where a reward expires on the game's clock and the span describes the schedule or the loss, code Playing by Appointment. Code FOMO only where the span describes anticipatory pressure i.e., the player continuing, returning, or feeling anxious in order not to miss out or fall behind. Both apply under R9 only if the span carries the schedule and the felt pressure.

A paid pass or subscription alone is Recurring Fee. Assign Playing by Appointment additionally only where the span describes the pass's clock operating on the player: tasks that must be completed before expiry, rewards forfeited by not playing within the window, or pressure to play to a schedule set by the pass. Price, duration, or poor value alone do not trigger it. Where both are present, assign both under R9.
Wait to Play requires the span to describe the wait or its regeneration schedule (lives/energy refilling over time, a build timer, a cooldown, a cooldown-skip offer).

counterexamples.text: The game itself seems to be good but after one day of play I decided to uninstall it. The reasons? 1. The controls in general are quite slow, even when you set sensibilities to its high 2. The matching times takes forever. I have been waiting for 5 min without starting a match. 3. The size of the maps in Royale are HUGE. Even if you choose the smallest map it takes forever to engage with enemies since the maps are that big.
counterexamples.why_not: Wait to Play requires a wait the game imposes as a gate like energy or lives regenerating, build and upgrade timers, cooldowns, cooldown-skip offers. Waits arising from the operation of the service rather than from a designed gate like matchmaking and queue times, loading, downloads, server latency, lag are not Playing by Appointment, however long the span says they last.

labels.canonical_definition: Motivates players to log in daily by providing incentives, while also penalising them for failing to do so.
indicators: Daily log-in reward calendars [indicators]
Daily task lists with resetting rewards [indicators]
(Alt. def.) (Hadan et al. 2024): “Patterns that encourage players to revisit the game daily.”
(Alt. def.) darkpattern.games: “Encourages return visits every day and punishes you for missing a day.”

Trapping starter kits: This pattern particularly entices new players to log in and play continuously for the first few
days after creating new accounts. These designs often use in-game rewards as incentives, creating
a situation where new players lose the opportunity to obtain these rewards if they fail to log in and
complete tasks within the specified timeframe. [dp-combo]

counterexamples.why_not: Assign only where the span describes the game rewarding the daily return or penalising a missed day: a login calendar, a resetting task list, a streak. A daily rate used by the reviewer to describe an exchange rate or earning ceiling ("100 coins a day takes 25 levels") measures the economy, it does not describe a daily-return incentive.

labels.canonical_definition: “Performing repetitive and tedious tasks” in order to make progress in a game. Emphasizes time invested over skill and in worst cases could be conducted unattended by the player.
indicators: (Alt. def.) (Hadan et al. 2024): “Patterns that requires players to perform repetitive tasks.”
(Alt. def.) (Sousa & Oliveira 2023): “Being compelled to complete monotonous tasks in order to make progress.”
(Alt. def.) (Dahlan & Susanty 2022): “It is forcing players to perform repetitive tasks to make progress in the game.”

Try now, Pay later (Zhang et. al): This pattern offers players the chance to initially try premium experiences,
powerful items, or privileges, with payment required at a later stage. [dp-combo]

Trapping starter kits: This pattern particularly entices new players to log in and play continuously for the first few
days after creating new accounts. These designs often use in-game rewards as incentives, creating
a situation where new players lose the opportunity to obtain these rewards if they fail to log in and
complete tasks within the specified timeframe. [dp-combo]

boundary_rules.rule: Assign where the span describes the activity required for progress as repetitive, tedious, or requiring the same task be repeated: replaying levels, farming, repeated attempts. A statement that progress is slow, hard, or time-consuming, without describing what the player must repeatedly do, is not Grinding on its own; where the slowness is attributed to payment being the alternative, code Pay to Progress alone.

Assign where the span identifies the repeated activity: replaying levels, farming, repeated attempts, a task cycle the player must run to advance. A general characterisation of the game as repetitive, boring, monotonous, or "the same thing over and over," with no activity named and no link to progress, is an evaluation of quality and codes NONE under R2.

labels.canonical_definition: Patterns that continually expand the game to never allow players to complete.
indicators: (Alt. def.) darkpattern.games: “Impossible to win or complete the game.”

boundary_rules.vs_label: High level number or long play history
boundary_rules.rule: Assign only where the span describes the game itself extending beyond completion: content added faster than it can be cleared, a goal that recedes as it is approached, no attainable end state, or the reviewer stating the game cannot be finished. A large level number, a high rank, a long tenure, or a report that the game "never ends" as a figure of speech for tedium is not sufficient.

labels.canonical_definition: Design that prevents the player from stopping at a moment of their choosing, requiring continuation to a stopping point defined by the game. Includes absent or restricted saving, checkpoint-only progress, and sessions or matches that cannot be exited without forfeiting progress.
indicators: Can’t Pause or Save (Hadan et al. 2024): “Patterns that force players to continue playing before they can save progress.” [low-level]

boundary_rules.rule: Mandatory Marathon requires that the player be prevented from ending a session or losing progress. Unskippable cutscenes, encounters, or animations within a session do not trigger it unless the review states the player could not stop playing or lost progress.

counterexamples.text: Revisiting this after a few years. Still annoyingly reliant on the user having a high-end phone. Adventure sync is good. Weird geographic limitations on pokemon feel ridiculous, but it's whatever. Wish spawn rates were higher in less populated areas, but I get it. Battles are fun.
counterexamples.why_not: "Unskippable encounters" specifies presence of elements that cannot be skipped but it is not related to progress.

labels.canonical_definition: Patterns that require the players to spend money to progress in-game.
labels.definition_citation: [NOT VERBATIM] Extracted from low level definitions.
indicators: Pay to Skip (Sousa & Oliveira 2023): “Permitting or actively promoting players to spend money to speed up their progress in the game.” Alt (Hadan 2024): “Patterns that allows players players to pay to bypass undesired obstacles.” Alt (Dahlan & Susanty 2022): “Allowing or even encouraging players to spend money to make progress in the game easier and faster.” darkpattern.games: “Spend money to avoid waiting for a timer to expire.” [low-level]

Pay to Win (Hadan et al. 2024): “Patterns that grant advantages to players who spend money.” Zagal et al.’s “Monetized Rivalries”: “Exploits Player competitiveness; encouraging them to spend money they would not otherwise in order to achieve in-game status such as a high placement on a leader board.” darkpattern.games: “A player can spend real money to purchase something that gives them an advantage in the game.” [low-level]

Pay Wall (Sousa & Oliveira 2023): “The game reaches a point where further progress is contingent on making a payment.” Alt (Hadan 2024): “Patterns that make the game unplayable without payment.” darkpattern.games: “The game becomes impossible to continue playing without payment.” [low-level]

Narrative Obligation (King et al. 2023): “the game’s narrative structure makes the purchase of in-game items a regular or repetitive part of gameplay. Although in-game currency may be earned, this is generally at a slow rate, so players may be forced to spend to keep the game flowing.” [low-level]

Try now, Pay later (Zhang et. al): This pattern offers players the chance to initially try premium experiences,
powerful items, or privileges, with payment required at a later stage. [dp-combo]

boundary_rules.rule: Pay to Progress holds whenever payment is described as a route past a progress obstacle, even if the reviewer names a free alternative (asking friends, waiting, watching an ad). The existence of a non-monetary bypass does not nullify the label; code the bypass separately if it satisfies its own label.

Where payment is described as removing, skipping, or unlocking a restriction rather than buying advancement, ad removal, inventory or loadout actions, convenience functions, assign Pay to Progress only where the span shows the restriction standing between the player and continued play or progress. Friction described purely as an annoyance, with no progress consequence in the span, does not trigger it.

labels.canonical_definition: Pattern where players use real-world money to acquire in-game currency for purchases or trades within the game world
indicators: Premium Currency (Sousa & Oliveira 2023): “The true cost of in-game items is concealed by the exchange rate between real-world currency and virtual currency.” Alt (Hadan 2024): “Patterns that disguises item real prices by introducing exchange rates.” darkpattern.games: “Exchange rate between real money and in-game currency disguises the real price of items.” [low-level]

Polymorphic Currency:is the use of multiple, purpose-specific in-game currencies within a
single game that can either be purchased with real-world money or earned by in-game activities.
The malicious part is that they are non-interchangeable. Zhang et al. 2025. [low-level]
Bulk Purchase: King et al. 2023: “the player may only purchase in-game currency in set pack sizes, with a bulk-buy discount to encourage larger purchases” [low-level]
Leftovers: King et al. 2023: “the pricing of items is not aligned to the pack sizes, meaning that players must often purchase more currency than required.” [low-level]

labels.canonical_definition: Deceptive Luxury is a game design tactic that makes an item feel rare and exclusive so players will pay more for it, when the rarity was invented by the developer rather than being a real limit. The item's price reflects manufactured scarcity, not genuine value.
indicators: Artificial Scarcity (Hadan et al. 2024): “Patterns that use limited-time offers to manipulate player decisions.” darkpattern.games: “Limited time offers with unnecessary urgency.” [low-level]

Remedy Consumption: is a pattern where players are given a second opportunity to correct
a missed purchase of some limited, valuable in-game items. This involves intentional artificial
scarcity for these in-game items, which compels players to expend additional effort or incur further
costs (compared to the first time) to obtain them. Zhang et al. 2025. [low-level]

Rarity Level (Zhang et al.): in-game items are often designed with varying levels of rarity. For
instance, character skins are ranked from B rank to S++ rank, with
higher ranks featuring more intricate designs and commanding higher prices [dp-enhancer]. Mention of rarity tied to price, purchase, or manufactured scarcity implies presence of pattern.

boundary_rules.rule: Deceptive Luxury requires the scarcity to bear on price or purchase. Availability restrictions with no monetary consequence in the span (regional exclusives, location-gated content, low spawn rates) are not Deceptive Luxury

counterexamples.text: after the new update whenever I switch to any of my mythic guns I just start lagging mid game, so many bugs in the game, now I can't use any of my mythic just legendarys and prestige guns, please fix this
counterexamples.why_not: Mention of rarity or tier names (mythic, legendary, S-rank, prestige) is a dp-enhancer, not a low-level indicator, and does not lift to Deceptive Luxury under R5. Require a span tying the rarity to price, purchase, or manufactured scarcity.

labels.canonical_definition: Patterns that encourages players to maximize playtime to justify their spending.
indicators: (Alt. def.) darkpattern.games: Involves monthly/yearly subscriptions which encourages the player to play as much as possible to get their money's worth.
Battle passes, MMO-subscriptions [indicators]

labels.canonical_definition: Using real money to participate in a game that involves an element of luck, with the possibility of receiving a prize as a reward.
indicators: Loot Boxes (Hadan 2024, “Gambling / Loot Boxes”): “Patterns that encourages players to spend money on chance-based rewards.” darkpattern.games (“Gambling / Loot Boxes”): “Spending real money to play a game of chance for a reward.” [low-level]

Risk Conversion: offers players an alternative way to achieve their goals, such as obtaining
an extremely rare item, by spending a substantial amount of money to circumvent the uncertainties
inherent in gambling mechanics. However, the actual amount players spend is significantly higher
than if they had opted for gambling mechanics. This pattern specifically targets risk-averse players. Zhang et al. 2025 [low-level]

Bundle Bonus: encourages players to engage in multiple gambling attempts at once rather
than a single one. For instance, if a player undertakes 10 in-game lottery activities at once, they
receive an additional opportunity for free, incentivizing bulk gambling. . Zhang et al. 2025. [low-level]

boundary_rules.rule: Where real money is converted into in-game currency and that currency is then wagered, assign both Gambling and Intermediate Currency under R9. The intervening currency layer does not nullify Gambling ("using real money" is satisfied by the funding chain), and the wagering does not absorb Intermediate Currency. Assign Gambling alone where the stake is currency earned in-game with no purchase described.

Gambling's real-money element must be present in the span. Naming gacha, loot boxes, crates, or a summon system, and describing their odds, establishes chance-based delivery but not a monetary stake, code Reward Mania. Assign Gambling where the span describes money spent, a purchased stake, or a described wager of earned currency (per the Intermediate Currency rule). Do not supply the monetary element from the fact that the mechanic is normally monetised.

labels.canonical_definition: Patterns that diminishing the value of purchased items over time to drive new purchases.
indicators: (Alt. def.) darkpattern.games: “A permanently purchased item in the game becomes less valuable over time.”

boundary_rules.rule: Power Creep requires the span to show a purchased item losing value after acquisition, through updates, new releases, or rebalancing. An item that is underpowered or unusable at the point of sale and requires further payment to reach full function is not Power Creep; code Pay to Progress where the further payment buys progress or advantage.

labels.canonical_definition: Patterns set small differences between in-game currency and item costs, prompting additional currency purchases.
indicators: (Alt. def.) darkpattern.games: “Capped inventory forces you to destroy items or upgrade inventory. Also, having small amounts of left over premium currency.”

labels.canonical_definition: Interface design that reduces the friction or deliberation involved in spending real money, through purchase-by-default options, absent confirmation or refund steps, prompts triggered at the point of insufficient funds, or price presentation that makes an amount appear smaller than it is.
labels.definition_citation: [NOT VERBATIM] Derived from low level defintions.
indicators: Anchoring Tricks (Hadan et al. 2024): “Patterns that place inexpensive items next to expensive ones to create the illusion of affordability.” darkpattern.games: “Placing a cheap item next to an expensive item to make it look more affordable.” [low-level]

Accidental Purchases (Hadan et al. 2024): “Patterns that use visual design or default options to deceive players into making unintended purchases.” darkpattern.games: “Making it easy to accidentally spend money with no confirmation or ability to undo or refund the action.” [low-level]

Low Barrier: King et al. 2023 “Default To Purchase”: “instances where the player was directed to purchase in-game items or in-game currency as a default action; if they do not wish to purchase, they must opt-out.” [low-level]

Prompted to Buy: King et al. 2023: “if the player attempts to buy an item with insufficient credit, the user interface displays a prompt for the user to purchase additional in-game currency with real money.” [low-level]

labels.canonical_definition: The user interface (i.e., not the NPC) contains elements designed to purposefully focus attention on specific options, or away from opportunities to opt-out.
indicators: Exciting UI Effect: King et al. 2023: “the use of colors and animation to direct the player’s attention to selected UI elements (such as the ‘buy in-game currency’ button)”; “[the buy button] was attracting more attention than the rest of the screen”; “a pleasing sound effect described as ‘an angelic choir’ and ‘a heavenly sound’ to accompany the appearance of the in-game currency storefront.” [low-level]

labels.canonical_definition: The “Never-Ending Lure” pattern is designed to convert non-paying players into paying ones (“First Charge Discount”) and encourage consistent long-term payments (“Accumulating Rewards”).
indicators: First Charge Discount: happens when in-game items or currencies are offered at significantly reduced prices for the player’s first purchase, and then revert to the original higher price for subsequent purchases. This pattern distorts the player’s perception of in-game items’ true value. Zhang et al. 2025.[low-level]
Accumulating Rewards: involves granting privileges, special offers, and rewards to players who spend above certain monetary thresholds. Zhang et al. 2025. [low-level]

boundary_rules.rule:
it focuses on a one-time-only purchase to mislead players into feeling
that they have taken advantage of the purchase unlike Premium Currency which is a permanent effect.

Unlike Pay to Win, where players directly spend
money to gain in-game advantages, this pattern does not emphasize helping players progress faster.
Instead, it offers players a special, privileged, and extraordinary status that is visible to other players.

labels.canonical_definition: Forced Fellowship is a game design tactic that turns real friendships into leverage: the game rewards you for pulling friends in, then makes it costly to stop playing because quitting would let those friends down.Design that uses the player's social ties, real or in-game, as the mechanism of recruitment or retention: rewarding the player for bringing others into the game, or making disengagement costly because absence burdens teammates, guildmates, or friends.
indicators: Social Pyramid Scheme (Sousa & Oliveira 2023): “Players are incentivized to invite friends to join the game and are encouraged to continue spreading the invitation to others in their social circle.” Alt (Hadan 2024): “Patterns that reward players for inviting friends.” Alt (Dahlan & Susanty 2022): “Encouraging or sometimes forcing players to invite people to join them in the game to gain in-game incentives or make progress.” darkpattern.games: “You get a bonus for inviting your friends and then they have to invite their friends.” [low-level]

Social Obligation / Guilds (Sousa & Oliveira 2023): “Due to a sense of responsibility towards one's friends, players may feel compelled to play the game even when they would prefer not to.” Alt (Hadan 2024): “Patterns that create a sense of obligation to avoid letting down friends in the game.” darkpattern.games: “To avoid letting down your friends, you are obligated to play when you don't want to.” [low-level]

boundary_rules.rule:
If the player is asked to bring NEW people into the game, code Forced Fellowship
  (Social Pyramid Scheme). If the player exchanges resources, lives, or favours with
  people ALREADY playing, code Reciprocity. If the player is described as playing
  when they'd rather not, so as not to burden others, code Forced Fellowship (Social Obligation).

Where the span shows the player compelled into a group to obtain protection or mechanical advantage against other players, or to obtain rewards with no obligation to those group members described, Forced Fellowship does not apply.

counterexamples.text: Nice distraction and my alliance is filled with lovely people!
counterexamples.why_not: Names an in-game social group without describing recruitment pressure or obligation to keep playing; the Social Obligation indicator requires the player be shown playing when they would rather not

labels.canonical_definition: Patterns that incentivize players to engage in dishonest or harmful actions to gain an advantage.
indicators: (Alt. def.) darkpattern.games: “The game incentivizes players to lie, cheat, or backstab other players to get ahead.”

boundary_rules.rule: Design that permits, enables, or fails to prevent players harming one another is not sufficient. Assign only where the span shows a reward, advantage, or incentive flowing to the player who acts harmfully: plunder taken, ranking or progression gained, rewards for deception or betrayal. Statements that developers "allow", "let it happen", or decline to intervene describe absent moderation, not incentive, and code NONE. Where the span carries both the harmful act and the gain it produces for the aggressor, assign the label.

labels.meso_label: Easy to Get, Hard to Lose
labels.canonical_definition: Design in which accumulated investment, time played, money spent, progress attained, or partially completed goals, raises the cost of leaving. Entry is low-friction; exit entails forfeiting value the player already holds.
labels.definition_citation: [NOT VERBATIM] Derived from low level defintions.
indicators: Invested (Endowed) Value (Sousa & Oliveira 2023): “Having invested significant time and money into advancing one's status in the game, it can be challenging to abandon those gains.” Alt (Hadan 2024): “Patterns that make it hard for players to discard investments in time and money.” darkpattern.games (“Invested / Endowed Value”): “Having already spent time and money to improve your status in the game, it's difficult to throw it away.” [low-level]

Endowed Progress (Hadan et al. 2024, “Badges / Endowed Progress”): “Patterns that discourage players from abandoning partially completed goals.” darkpattern.games (“Badges / Endowed Progress”): “Reluctancy to abandon a partially completed goal, even one forced upon the player.” [low-level]

Try now, Pay later (Zhang et. al): This pattern offers players the chance to initially try premium experiences,
powerful items, or privileges, with payment required at a later stage. [dp-combo]

labels.canonical_definition: Patterns that deceive players about their skill level to encourage more gameplay.
indicators: (Alt. def.) darkpattern.games: “The game cheats or hides information to make you think you're better than you actually are.”

boundary_rules.rule: Assign where the span asserts that the game conceals or manipulates the determination of outcomes, a non-random deal, a fixed win ratio, engineered near-misses, matchmaking or difficulty tuned to a hidden schedule, whether the deception is framed as being about the player's skill or about the game's odds. Do not assign from an unlucky or losing run alone, or from a general accusation of unfairness with no mechanism described in the span. Loss streaks also encourage more gameplay.

Where the span asserts that the game determines or tunes outcomes: a non-random deal, a fixed win ratio, difficulty or matchmaking on a hidden schedule, code Illusion of Control. Where the span describes the player's perception of frequency: near-wins felt as frequent, a run of almost-successes, a sense that a win is imminent, code Optimism and Frequency Biases. Engineered near-misses commonly carry both: the alleged design (IoC) and the perceptual effect it produces (O&FB). Assign both under R9 only where the span carries the manipulation claim and the frequency perception; a near-miss reported without any claim of manipulation is O&FB alone.

labels.canonical_definition: Reward structures in which the mechanism of delivery, its complexity, its unpredictability, or the out-of-game activity it demands, is what sustains engagement, rather than the value of the reward itself. The player invests disproportionate cognitive effort, repeated attempts, or external activity in pursuit of the reward system.
indicators:
Overloading (Zhang et al.):occurs in in-game mechanisms, such as reward systems or gambling, that are
designed to be overly complex, thereby enticing players to invest significant effort in understanding
and engaging with them. [low-level]

Sycophant (Zhang et al.): “Sycophant” refers to the use of rewards within the game to encourage players to allocate
additional attention and resources to social activities outside of the game, such as following the
game’s social media accounts or participating in related online communities. [low-level]

Variable Rewards (Sousa & Oliveira 2023): “Irregular or unexpected rewards have a greater potential to generate addiction compared to rewards provided on a predictable schedule.” Alt (Hadan 2024): “Patterns that offer unpredictable or random rewards to enhance game addiction.” darkpattern.games: “Unpredictable or random rewards are more addictive than a predictable schedule.” [low-level]
Gacha mechanics [indicators]

labels.canonical_definition: “Fragmented Downloads” are characterized by designs that obscure the true storage requirements of the game until the game starts. This is deceptive because it targets mobile users who are cautious about their device’s storage capacity and foments a space monopoly by the app against competitors.
indicators: Small advertised App Store size vs. large mandatory in-game download [indicators]
“Download wall” blocking progress past the tutorial [indicators]
Missing animations / assets with in-place “downloading” prompts when packages are declined [indicators]
